4.1.title: Therapeutic indications
4.1.text: Povofortay is indicated for the treatment of active moderate to severe hidradenitis suppurativa (acne inversa) in adults who have responded inadequately to, or who are intolerant or contraindicated to an anti-TNF therapy.

4.2.title: Posology and method of administration
4.2.text:
Treatment should be initiated and supervised by a physician experienced in the diagnosis and treatment of hidradenitis suppurativa.

Posology

The dose is 45 mg or 75 mg once daily based on individual patient characteristics:

•        A dose of 45 mg once daily is recommended for patients at higher risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE), major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and malignancy (see section 4.4).
•        A dose of 75 mg once daily may be appropriate for patients with high disease burden who are not at higher risk of VTE, MACE and malignancy (see section 4.4)
•        A dose of 75 mg once daily may also be appropriate for patients with an inadequate response to 45 mg once daily.
•        The lowest effective dose to maintain response should be used.

Consideration should be given to discontinuing treatment in patients who have shown no evidence of therapeutic benefit after 12 weeks of treatment. Patients with an initial partial response at week 12 may subsequently improve with continued treatment.

If retreatment with povorcitinib is indicated, the above guidance on dose and treatment duration should be followed.

Treatment initiation Treatment with povorcitinib should not be initiated in patients with a platelet count < 50 × 109/L, an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) < 1 × 103/mm3, or who have a haemoglobin value < 8 g/dL (see section 4.4).

Treatment interruption If a patient develops a serious infection, treatment should be interrupted until the infection is controlled (see section 4.4).

Missed doses If a dose is missed, patients should be advised to take the dose as soon as possible unless it is less than 12 hours before the next dose, in which case the patient should not take the missed dose. Thereafter, dosing should be resumed at the regular scheduled time.

Interactions For patients receiving chronic treatment with strong systemic CYP3A4 inhibitors, the recommended dose is 45 mg once daily (see section 4.5).

Co-administration of povorcitinib with chronic use of strong systemic CYP3A4 inducers is not recommended (see section 4.5).

Special populations

Elderly For patients 65 years of age and older, the recommended dose is 45 mg once daily (see section 4.4).

Renal impairment No dose adjustment is required in patients with renal impairment, including patients with end stage renal disease (ESRD) (see section 5.2).

Hepatic impairment No dose adjustment is required in patients with mild (Child-Pugh A) or moderate (Child-Pugh B) hepatic impairment (see section 5.2). For patients with severe (Child-Pugh C) hepatic impairment, the maximum recommended dose is 45 mg once daily (see section 5.2).

Paediatric population There is no relevant use of povorcitinib in children under 12 years of age for the treatment of hidradenitis suppurativa.

The safety and efficacy of povorcitinib in children and adolescents between 12 and less than 18 years of age have not yet been established. No data are available.

Method of administration

For oral use.

Tablets can be taken with or without food. Tablets should be swallowed whole and should not be split, crushed or chewed.

4.3.title: Contraindications
4.3.text: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1. Active serious systemic infections, including active tuberculosis (TB) (see section 4.4). Pregnancy and breast-feeding (see section 4.6).

4.4.title: Special warnings and precautions for use
4.4.text:
Povorcitinib should only be used if no suitable treatment alternatives are available in patients:
- 65 years of age and older;
- patients with history of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease or other cardiovascular risk factors (such as current or past long-time smokers);
- patients with malignancy risk factors (e.g. current malignancy or history of malignancy).

Serious infections

Infections, including serious infections, have been reported in patients receiving povorcitinib (see section 4.8).

As there is a higher incidence of infections in elderly and in the diabetic population in general, caution should be used when treating the elderly and patients with diabetes. In patients 65 years of age and older, povorcitinib should only be used if no suitable treatment alternatives are available (see section 4.2).

Treatment with povorcitinib must not be initiated in patients with an active, serious infection (see section 4.3).

Risks and benefits of treatment prior to initiating povorcitinib should be considered for patients:
•     with chronic or recurrent infections
•     who have been exposed to tuberculosis (TB)
•     with a history of a serious or an opportunistic infection
•     who have resided or travelled in areas of endemic TB or endemic mycoses; or
•     with underlying conditions that may predispose them to infection.

Patients should be closely monitored for the development of signs and symptoms of infection during and after treatment with povorcitinib. A patient who develops a new infection during treatment should undergo prompt and complete diagnostic testing and appropriate antimicrobial therapy should be initiated. The patient should be closely monitored, and povorcitinib therapy should be interrupted if the patient is not responding to standard therapy. Povorcitinib may be resumed once the infection is controlled.

Tuberculosis Patients should be screened for TB before starting povorcitinib therapy. Povorcitinib must not be given to patients with active TB (see section 4.3). Anti-TB therapy should be considered prior to initiation of povorcitinib in patients with previously untreated latent TB or in patients with risk factors for TB infection. Patients should be monitored for the development of signs and symptoms of TB.

Viral reactivation Viral reactivation, including cases of herpes virus reactivation (e.g. herpes zoster) was reported in clinical studies (see section 4.8). If a patient develops herpes zoster, interruption of treatment should be considered until the episode resolves.

Screening for viral hepatitis and monitoring for reactivation should be performed in accordance with clinical guidelines before starting and during treatment with povorcitinib. Patients with evidence of hepatitis B or C infection were excluded from studies with povorcitinib. If there is evidence of reactivation, a liver specialist should be consulted.

Malignancy

Malignancies have been reported in patients receiving JAK inhibitors, including povorcitinib.

In a large randomised active-controlled study of tofacitinib (another oral JAK inhibitor) in rheumatoid arthritis patients 50 years and older with at least one additional cardiovascular risk factor, a higher rate of malignancies, particularly lung cancer, lymphoma and non-melanoma skin cancer (NMSC), was observed with tofacitinib compared to tumour necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors.

In patients over 65 years of age, patients who are current or past long-time smokers, or with other malignancy risk factors (e.g. current malignancy or history of malignancy), povorcitinib should only be used if no suitable treatment alternatives are available.

Non-melanoma skin cancer (NMSC) NMSCs have been reported in patients treated with povorcitinib. Periodic skin examination is recommended for all patients, particularly those who are at increased risk for skin cancer.

Venous thromboembolism (VTE)

Events of deep venous thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE) have been reported in patients receiving povorcitinib.

In a large randomised active-controlled study of tofacitinib (another JAK inhibitor) in rheumatoid arthritis patients 50 years and older with at least one additional cardiovascular risk factor, a dose-dependent higher rate of VTE including DVT and PE was observed with tofacitinib compared to TNF inhibitors.

In patients with cardiovascular or malignancy risk factors (see also section 4.4 “Major adverse cardiovascular events” and “Malignancy”) povorcitinib should only be used if no suitable treatment alternatives are available.

In patients with known VTE risk factors other than cardiovascular or malignancy risk factors, povorcitinib should be used with caution. VTE risk factors other than cardiovascular or malignancy risk factors include previous VTE, patients undergoing major surgery, immobilisation, use of combined hormonal contraceptives or hormone replacement therapy, inherited coagulation disorder.

Patients should be re-evaluated periodically during povorcitinib treatment to assess for changes in VTE risk.

Promptly evaluate patients with signs and symptoms of VTE and discontinue povorcitinib in patients with suspected VTE, regardless of dose.

Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE)

Events of MACE have been observed in patients taking povorcitinib.

In a large randomised active-controlled study of tofacitinib (another JAK inhibitor) in rheumatoid arthritis, patients 50 years and older with at least one additional cardiovascular risk factor, a higher rate of MACE, defined as cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction and non-fatal stroke was observed with tofacitinib compared to TNF inhibitors.

Therefore, in patients 65 years of age and older, patient who are current or past long-time smokers and patients with history of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease or other cardiovascular risk factors, povorcitinib should only be used if no suitable treatment alternatives are available.

Haematological abnormalities

Platelet counts of < 50 × 109/L, an ANC < 1× 103/mm3, and haemoglobin < 8 g/dL were reported in the povorcitinib clinical studies. Treatment should not be initiated, or should be interrupted in patients with platelet counts < 50 × 109/L, an ANC < 1 × 103/mm3 or haemoglobin < 8 g/dL (see section 4.2). Complete blood count should be monitored before treatment initiation and thereafter according to individual patient management (see section 4.2).

Lipids

Dose-dependent increases in blood lipid parameters were reported in patients treated with povorcitinib compared to placebo. Patients with abnormal lipid parameters should be further monitored and managed according to clinical guidelines (see section 4.2). The effect of these lipid parameter elevations on cardiovascular morbidity and mortality has not been determined.

Vaccination

No data are available on the response to vaccination in patients receiving povorcitinib. Use of live, attenuated vaccines should be avoided during or immediately prior to treatment. Prior to initiating treatment with this medicinal product, it is recommended that patients are brought up to date with all immunisations, including prophylactic herpes zoster vaccinations, in agreement with current immunisation guidelines.

Use in patients 65 years of age and older

Considering the increased risk of MACE, malignancies, serious infections, and all-cause mortality in patients 65 years of age and older, as observed in a large, randomised study of tofacitinib (another JAK inhibitor), povorcitinib should only be used in these patients if no suitable treatment alternatives are available.

Immunosuppressive medicinal products

Combination with biologic immunomodulators, potent immunosuppressants such as ciclosporin or other Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors has not been studied. Their concomitant use with povorcitinib is not recommended as a risk of additive immunosuppression cannot be excluded.

Combination with strong CYP3A4 inducers

Co-administration of povorcitinib with chronic use of strong systemic CYP3A4 inducers is not recommended (see section 4.5).

Excipients with known effect

Sodium This medicinal product contains less than 1 mmol sodium (23 mg) per tablet, that is to say essentially ‘sodium-free’.

4.8.text:

The most commonly reported adverse reactions are upper respiratory tract infections (14.0%) and acne (11.1%).

Description of selected adverse reactions

Infections In placebo-controlled studies (STOP-HS1 and STOP-HS2), for up to 12 weeks, infections were reported in 28.2% of patients treated with povorcitinib 45 mg, 35% of patients treated with povorcitinib 75 mg, and 24.9% of patients treated with placebo. The majority of infections were non- serious, mild to moderate in severity, and did not lead to discontinuation of povorcitinib. The incidence of patients reporting infection-related adverse reactions in the 45 mg and 75 mg groups compared to placebo were: upper respiratory tract infections (13.3% and 14.7% versus 10.1%), folliculitis (1.2% and 3.7% versus 1%), urinary tract infection (3.4% and 2.2% versus 1.5%), herpes zoster (0.5% and 0.7% versus 0%). In the overall treatment period, for up to 54 weeks, infections were reported in 49.2% of patients (65.2 per 100 patient-years) treated with povorcitinib 45 mg and 55.1% of patients (71.9 per 100 patient-years) treated with povorcitinib 75 mg.

In placebo-controlled studies (STOP-HS1 and STOP-HS2), most of the herpes zoster events involved a single dermatome and were non-serious, mild to moderate in severity and did not lead to

discontinuation of povorcitinib. For up to 12 weeks, the incidence rate of herpes zoster in patients treated with povorcitinib 45 mg was 2.2 per 100 patient-years, in patients treated with 75 mg was 3.3 per 100 patient-years, and in patients treated with placebo was 0 per 100 patient-years. In the overall treatment period, for up to 54 weeks, the incidence rate of herpes zoster in patients treated with povorcitinib 45 mg was 2.5 per 100 patient-years and in patients treated with 75 mg was 2.6 per 100 patient-years.

In placebo-controlled studies (STOP-HS1 and STOP-HS2), for up to 12 weeks, the incidence rate of serious infections was 0 per 100 patient-years in patients treated with povorcitinib 45 mg, 2.2 per 100 patient-years in patients treated with 75 mg, and in patients treated with placebo was 6.6 per 100 patient-years. In the overall treatment period, for up to 54 weeks, the incidence rate of serious infections in patients treated with povorcitinib 45 mg was 1.1 per 100 patient-years and in patients treated with 75 mg was 2.6 per 100 patient-years.

CPK elevation In placebo-controlled studies (STOP-HS1 and STOP-HS2), for up to 12 weeks, blood creatine phosphokinase (CPK) increased were reported in 3.2% of patients treated with povorcitinib 45 mg, 2.7% of patients treated with povorcitinib 75 mg, and 0.7% of patients treated with placebo. Most elevations were transient and none led to discontinuation.

Lipid elevations In placebo-controlled studies (STOP-HS1 and STOP-HS2), for up to 12 weeks, there was a dose- related increase in low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-c), total cholesterol, and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-c) relative to placebo. Elevations were observed within 6 weeks and remained stable thereafter, through week 54. There was no meaningful change in the HDL/LDL ratio or in the triglyceride levels in patients treated with povorcitinib relative to patients treated with placebo. Events related to hyperlipidaemia occurred in 2.7% of patients exposed to povorcitinib 45 mg, 2.0% of patients exposed to 75 mg and 2.2% of patients exposed to placebo and none led to discontinuation (see section 4.4).

Neutropenia In placebo-controlled studies (STOP-HS1 and STOP-HS2), for up to 12 weeks, neutropenia occurred in 0.2% of patients treated with 75 mg, and 0.0% of patients treated with 45 mg or placebo. Dose- related changes in neutrophil counts were transient, and observed within 3 weeks, after which the neutrophil count returned towards baseline despite continued therapy. There was no clear relationship between neutropenia and the occurrence of serious infections.

Thrombocytopenia In placebo-controlled studies (STOP-HS1 and STOP-HS2), for up to 12 weeks, thrombocytopenia occurred in 1.0% of patients treated with 75 mg, and 0.0% of patients treated with 45 mg or placebo. Dose-related changes in platelet counts were transient, and observed within 3 weeks, after which the platelet count returned towards baseline despite continued therapy.

Increased transaminases In placebo-controlled studies (STOP-HS1 and STOP-HS2), for up to 12 weeks, events of increased ALT values (> 3 × ULN) occurred in 0.7% of patients treated with 75 mg, and 0.2% of patients treated with 45 mg, and 0.0% of patients treated with placebo. Increased AST values (> 3 × ULN) occurred in 0.5% of patients treated with 75 mg or 45 mg and 0.2% of patients treated with placebo. Most elevations were transient.

Reporting of suspected adverse reactions Reporting suspected adverse reactions after authorisation of the medicinal product is important. It allows continued monitoring of the benefit/risk balance of the medicinal product. Healthcare professionals are asked to report any suspected adverse reactions via the national reporting system listed in Appendix V.

5.1.title: Pharmacodynamic properties
5.1.text:
Pharmacotherapeutic group: Immunosuppressants, Janus-associated kinase (JAK) inhibitors, ATC code: not yet assigned

Mechanism of action

Povorcitinib is a Janus kinase (JAK) 1 inhibitor. JAK1 is a member of the JAK family of intracellular enzymes, which also includes JAK2, JAK3, and tyrosine kinase 2 (TYK2). JAKs transmit signals arising from cytokine- or growth factor-receptor interactions on the cell membrane. Within the signalling pathway, JAKs phosphorylate and activate signal transducers and activators of transcription (STATs) which modulate gene expression. This influences cellular processes of immune cell function and haematopoiesis depending on the specific JAK isoforms involved. Povorcitinib modulates the JAK1 signalling pathway, preventing the phosphorylation and activation of associated STATs. By inhibiting immune cell activation by JAK1-dependent cytokines (such as IL-6, IL-2, IL-22) povorcitinib attenuates skin and systemic inflammation relevant to hidradenitis suppurativa.

Pharmacodynamic effects

Inhibition of IL-6 induced STAT3 phosphorylation In healthy volunteers, oral administration of povorcitinib resulted in dose-dependent inhibition of IL- 6–induced pSTAT3, a pharmacodynamic marker of JAK1 signalling. Maximal inhibition was observed between 1 and 6 hours after administration.

High-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP) Decreases from baseline in serum hsCRP, an inflammatory marker primarily induced by IL-6 signaling through the JAK1 pathway were observed with povorcitinib as early as the first study visit (week 3).

Cardiac electrophysiology The QT interval prolongation potential of povorcitinib was assessed in healthy subjects who received a single dose of 450 mg povorcitinib in a placebo- and positive-controlled thorough QT study. No clinically relevant effect on the QTc interval was observed.

Clinical efficacy and safety

The efficacy and safety of povorcitinib were evaluated in 1227 adult patients with moderate to severe hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) in two Phase 3 multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo- controlled studies, STOP-HS1 and STOP-HS2. Patients had a diagnosis of HS (Hurley Stage II or III) for at least 3 months and were required to have at least 5 inflammatory lesions (i.e. number of abscesses plus number of inflammatory nodules) affecting at least 2 anatomical areas at baseline.

Patients had a history of inadequate response to a 3-month or longer course of 1 or more conventional systemic therapy (oral antibiotic or biologic medicinal product) for HS or demonstrated intolerance to or had a contraindication to a conventional systemic therapy for HS. All patients received prior systemic treatment; of which 96% had received prior oral antibiotic therapy and 37% had received prior biologic therapy (predominantly adalimumab). A total of 330 patients comprised the pooled post- anti-TNF population, defined as a history of inadequate response to a 3-month or longer course of 1 or more anti-TNF biologic drug for HS or demonstrated intolerance to or had a contraindication to an anti-TNF biologic drug for HS.

In STOP-HS1 and STOP-HS2, patients were randomised 1:1:1 to receive povorcitinib 45 mg once daily, povorcitinib 75 mg once daily for 54 weeks, or placebo once daily up to week 12 followed by povorcitinib 45 mg once daily or povorcitinib 75 mg once daily up to week 54. To evaluate the use of povorcitinib as monotherapy, concomitant systemic antibiotic use for HS was not permitted during the placebo-controlled period, except for rescue (imputed as non-responders).

The primary endpoint in both studies was the proportion of patients achieving Hidradenitis Suppurativa Clinical Response 50 (HiSCR50) at week 12, i.e., at least a 50% reduction in the total abscess and inflammatory nodule count with no increase in abscess or draining tunnel count relative to baseline. Key secondary endpoints included the proportion of patients who achieved HiSCR75 at week 12, the proportion of patients achieving Skin Pain NRS30 at week 12 among patients with baseline Skin Pain numerical rating scale (NRS) score ≥ 3, and the proportion of patients with a flare by week 12.

Pre-planned analyses provide data on the indicated post-anti-TNF population. STOP-HS1 evaluated 608 patients and STOP-HS2 evaluated 619 patients, of whom 154 patients (25.3%) and 176 patients (28.4%), respectively, represented the post-anti-TNF population. Baseline characteristics for this group were consistent across both studies and reflective of a population with moderate to severe HS. In the pooled post-anti-TNF population, the most commonly received prior biologic therapy was adalimumab and 87.6% of patients had received prior oral antibiotic therapy. Patients had a mean disease duration of 12.3 years. The proportions of Hurley Stage II and Stage III patients were 52% (48.7% in STOP-HS1 and 55.1% in STOP-HS2) and 48% (51.3% in STOP-HS1 and 44.9% in STOP- HS2) respectively. The mean abscess and inflammatory nodule (AN) count was 14.4 and the mean number of draining tunnels was 3.7. The mean Skin Pain NRS score was 6.0. 63% of patients were female, and the mean age of all patients was 38.6 years. 73% of patients were White, and 14% were Black or African American. Most patients were current (45.5%) or former (17.9%) smokers and had a BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2 (61.5%).

Clinical response in the post-anti-TNF population Treatment with povorcitinib resulted in improvement in disease activity compared to placebo at week 12 (Table 3). In the pooled post-anti-TNF population, the proportion of patients achieving HiSCR50 at week 12 was greater in the povorcitinib 45 and 75 mg groups than in the placebo group (Table 3). Clinical responses were sustained through week 54.

Paediatric population

The European Medicines Agency has deferred the obligation to submit the results of studies with Povofortay in one or more subsets of the paediatric population in the treatment of HS (see section 4.2 for information on paediatric use).

5.2.title: Pharmacokinetic properties
5.2.text:
Absorption

Following oral single-dose or multiple-dose administration, povorcitinib is absorbed with a median Tmax of 2 to 4 hours. Steady state plasma concentrations are achieved within 9 days with an accumulation ratio of 2.2 to 2.6 -fold. Coadministration of povorcitinib with a high-fat meal had no clinically relevant effect on povorcitinib exposures at the 45 mg or 75 mg dose level (increased AUC0- ∞ by 8% to 14% and Cmax by 6% to 13%). In clinical trials, povorcitinib was administered without regard to meals. Based on population pharmacokinetic analysis, povorcitinib pharmacokinetics were linear across the evaluated dose range (6 mg to 225 mg).

Medicinal product concentrations in skin In healthy subjects, following oral administration of povorcitinib 75 mg once daily, concentrations of the medicinal product in skin tissue and plasma were similar for at least 7 days (168 hours) after the last dose.

Distribution

Povorcitinib is highly bound to plasma proteins, with a human ex vivo unbound fraction of 6.4%. Povorcitinib has limited distribution into blood cells, with a blood-to-plasma total radioactivity ratio of 0.656 to 0.887. Povorcitinib is highly bound to skin proteins, with an unbound fraction of 4.2% in dermatomed (epidermis plus dermis) human skin homogenate. Based on population pharmacokinetic analysis, the estimated apparent volume of distribution (Vd/F) was 285.9 L in HS patients.

Biotransformation

The in vitro CYP phenotyping and metabolite profiling results showed that povorcitinib was mainly metabolised by CYP3A4, with lesser contributions from UGT1A4 and UGT1A3. In a human radiolabelled study, unchanged povorcitinib accounted for 69.3% of the total radioactivity in plasma while the only major metabolite (M12, product of N-glucuronidation of the dimethyl pyrazole moiety) accounted for 25.9% of the total circulating radioactivity. The pharmacologic activity of povorcitinib is attributed to the parent molecule. No active metabolites have been identified for povorcitinib.

Elimination

Following single oral administration of [14C]-povorcitinib, radioactivity was mainly excreted in faeces (59.2%) and lower amout in urine (30.6%). Intact povorcitinib was the most abundant analyte detected in human excreta (7.1% in urine and 29.1% in faeces), while the most abundant metabolite (M3, product of hydroxylation of the dimethyl bipyrazole moiety) comprised 12% of the administrated dose. Povorcitinib mean terminal elimination half-life ranged from 27 to 35 hours.

Special populations

Body weight, age, gender, and ethnicity Body weight, age, gender, race, and ethnicity did not have a clinically meaningful effect on povorcitinib exposure.

Renal impairment Povorcitinib Cmax was 21% lower while AUC was 20% higher in subjects with severe renal impairment (estimated glomerular filtration rate 15 to 29 ml/min/1.73 m2) compared with subjects with normal renal function, where eGFR was calculated using Modification of Diet in Renal Disease (MDRD) formula. These changes in exposure are not considered clinically relevant. No dose adjustment is required in subjects with mild, moderate, or severe renal impairment (estimated glomerular filtration rate 15 to 89 ml/min/1.73 m2).

In subjects with ESRD, povorcitinib Cmax was 36% and 31% lower, and AUC was 40% and 26% lower before and after haemodialysis, respectively, compared to subjects with normal renal function. Haemodialysis had no impact on povorcitinib pharmacokinetics. These changes in exposure are not considered clinically relevant and there is no safety concern based on the slightly lower plasma exposure.

No dose adjustment is required in subjects with ESRD, including those receiving haemodialysis.

Hepatic impairment Plasma povorcitinib (total or unbound) AUC and Cmax were similar for subjects with moderate hepatic impairment compared with healthy subjects with normal hepatic function. No dose adjustment is required for subjects with mild or moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh Classes A and B).

In subjects with severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh Class C), unbound povorcitinib Cmax and AUC were approximately 40% and 76% higher, respectively, compared to subjects with normal hepatic function. Due to the increased unbound exposure, the maximum recommended dose in subjects with severe hepatic impairment is 45 mg per day (see section 4.2).
